teach.title: What a wish looks like
teach.say: A wish in Latin is **utinam + subjunctive (the 'if only …' wish; the tense says whether it can still come true)**. The word *utinam* stands in front and the verb goes into the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do). *Utinam* is not one English word: it is the 'if only' or 'may …!' colouring. In wu-01 the verb is *veniat*, not *venit* — nobody is saying father is coming, only wishing it.

check.ask: Tap the verb that carries the wish.

teach.title: A wish that may still come true: the present subjunctive
teach.say: The tense says how possible the wish is. The present subjunctive leaves the door open: it may yet happen. Its mark is a changed vowel in the ending. In the first conjugation the *a* turns to *e*: *laudat* (he praises) becomes *laudet* (may he praise). Everywhere else it runs the other way about: *audit* becomes *audiat*, *ignōscit* becomes *ignōscat*. Either way the ending is not the one a plain statement uses.

check.ask: laudet — which tense and mood is it?

teach.title: A wish about now that cannot come true: the imperfect subjunctive
teach.say: Step back one tense and the wish turns regretful: the imperfect subjunctive says the thing is not so now. The third person singular is *audīret* — the whole infinitive *audīre* with **-t** on the end. Even *sum* does it: *esse* + **-m** gives *essem*. English steps back in time in the same way: 'if only I *were* rich'.

check.ask: essem — which tense is it, and so is the speaker in Rome or not?

teach.title: A wish about the past: the pluperfect subjunctive
teach.say: For a regret about what is already over, go back one tense further. The third person singular is *audīvisset* — the perfect stem *audīv-* plus **-isset**. Look for **-isse-** in the middle of the word: that is the mark of a wish about the past, and it means the thing did not happen.

check.ask: mānsisset — which tense is it, and so did Quintus stay or not?

teach.title: Wishing for something not to happen: utinam nē
teach.say: A negative wish takes *nē*, never *nōn*: **utinam nē**. Nothing else changes — *nē* simply slips in after *utinam*, and the verb keeps whichever of the three tenses the time calls for.

check.ask: Tap the verb that nē has made negative.

teach.title: Choosing the tense, and not mistaking a wish for an 'if'
teach.say: The same imperfect and pluperfect subjunctives appear in *sī* sentences — *sī Rōmae essem, laetus essem*. The opening word tells you which you have: *utinam* opens a wish and stops there, *sī* opens a condition whose second half draws the consequence. Once you know it is a wish, pick the tense by the time you mean.

check.ask: The same wish, but about the past: fill the blank with the pluperfect subjunctive of videō.

core.text: A wish is **utinam + subjunctive (the 'if only …' wish; the tense says whether it can still come true)**. *Utinam veniat!* — may he come, if only he comes (still possible: present subjunctive). *Utinam venīret!* — if only he were coming (he isn't: imperfect subjunctive). *Utinam vēnisset!* — if only he had come (he didn't: pluperfect subjunctive). The negative is *utinam nē*. Latin name: *coniūnctīvus optātīvus cum utinam*.
English: *may you be happy* (possible); *if only I were rich* (I'm not); *if only I had known* (I didn't). English also steps back in time to say 'impossible': *were*, *had*.
utinam (nē) + present = a hope; + imperfect = an impossible wish about now; + pluperfect = an impossible wish about the past.

invented.en: If only I were with you!

core.text: The same imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive appear in 'if I were …, I would …' sentences. The difference is *utinam* (or a bare wish) against *sī* plus a second clause that draws the consequence: *utinam Rōmae essem* (wish) but *sī Rōmae essem, laetus essem* (condition).

more.text: Also easy to confuse: *vīvāmus, amēmus* (let us live, let us love) and *valeat* (may he fare well) are wishes and exhortations in the present subjunctive without *utinam*. *Utinam* only makes the wish explicit; the imperfect and pluperfect never appear in the 'let us / let him' type.

The learner's notes (Week 33, 'Contrafactual Optative'): a present optative is a wish about the future that is technically possible even if unlikely (*amīcī veniant!* would that my friends came!); an imperfect optative is a wish about the present that is contrary to fact, and *utinam* is used especially then (*utinam ambulāre possem!* would that I could walk!; *utinam tempus esset discēdendī!*); a pluperfect optative is a contrary-to-fact wish about the past (*utinam numquam nātus essem!*, *utinam nē vēnissem!*).

Softer wishes use *velim* (I would like) and *vellem* (I wish, I would have liked): *vellem sī magis esset anus* — I'd wish it, if she were more of an old woman (Martial, Week 14). Ørberg's chapter 32 gives Medus's *utinam salvī perveniant!* and Lydia's wish to see, *līber*, *patriam* again; chapter 33 turns to the impossible: *utinam ego Rōmae essem!*
